        Steps:
        1. clone the repo git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
        2. analyse the contents of the repo and create following.

function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run commands or push code directly to your GitHub account, but I can walk you through each step and give you the exact files you’ll need to create or modify.  
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) and the content for the new/updated files.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you prefer HTTPS, replace the URL with `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git` and use your credentials.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create/update files

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick check to see what the repo contains:

```bash
# List top‑level files
ls -la

# Show the main entry point (if any)
cat package.json | grep -E '"main"|\"start\"' -A 5
```

Typical findings for a Node.js repo:

| File | Typical purpose |
|------|-----------------|
| `package.json` | Defines dependencies, scripts, start command |
| `app.js` / `index.js` | Main server file |
| `.env.example` | Example environment variables |
| `README.md` | Project description |

If the repo already has a `Dockerfile`, we’ll update it; otherwise we’ll create one.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` in the repo root (or overwrite the existing one):

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set the working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package.json and package-lock.json first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install production dependencies only
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on (adjust if your app uses a different port)
EXPOSE 3000

# Define the command to run the app
CMD ["npm", "start"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the latest LTS Node version.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs from `package-lock.json`.  
> * `--only=production` keeps the image slim by excluding dev dependencies.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the typical Express default; change if your app uses another port.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML files

Create a directory called `k8s` (or `deployments`) to hold the YAMLs:

```bash
mkdir -p k8s
```

#### Deployment (`k8s/deployment.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_DOCKER_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: nodejs-welcome-secrets   # optional: use a secret for env vars
```

#### Service (`k8s/service.yaml`)

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: LoadBalancer   # change to NodePort or ClusterIP if you prefer
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # external port
    targetPort: 3000  # container port
```

> **Tip:** If you’re deploying to a cluster that doesn’t support `LoadBalancer` (e.g., Minikube), switch to `NodePort`.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build and Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main   # trigger on pushes to main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - name: Checkout source
      uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Cache Docker layers
      uses: actions/cache@v3
      with:
        path: /tmp/.buildx-cache
        key: ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-${{ github.sha }}
        restore-keys: |
          ${{ runner.os }}-buildx-

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        push: true
        tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to set up:**
> 1. Create a Docker Hub account (or use GitHub Packages).  
> 2. In the repo settings → Secrets → Actions, add:
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a personal access token with `write:packages` scope

---

## 3️⃣ Add all changed files to git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/*.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

If you modified an existing `Dockerfile`, just add that file again.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit and push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run, build the image, and push it to Docker Hub.

---

### Quick checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ✅ | `Dockerfile` created/updated |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` added |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml` added |
| ✅ | Secrets set in GitHub repo settings |
| ✅ | Files committed and pushed |

That’s it! Once the workflow finishes, you’ll have a Docker image ready for deployment, and the Kubernetes manifests are ready to apply with `kubectl apply -f k8s/`. Let me know if you’d like help applying them to a specific cluster or configuring environment variables.
